n: Jesus gives his twelve disciples the same power he has been using — over evil spirits and every disease. Authority to act for him is formally given, not assumed.
Matthew lists the Twelve Apostles in pairs. Peter always comes first in these lists, reflecting his role as their leader.

f.g: Greek apostolos — “one who is sent,” an authorized messenger.

f.w: The first, Simon, who is called Peter

n: The list continues. Matthew humbly identifies himself as “the publican,” remembering the despised job he left to follow Jesus.

f.g: Probably the same apostle Luke calls Judas the brother (or son) of James.
Often identified with Nathanael.

n: The list ends with a sobering note: Judas Iscariot, “who also betrayed him.” Even among the chosen, agency remains.

f.g: From Aramaic qan’an, “zealous” — Luke calls him Simon Zelotes.
Possibly “man of Kerioth,” a town in Judea.

n: For this first mission, Jesus tells the Twelve not to go to Gentiles or Samaritans. The gospel would go first to Israel and later to all the world.

f.w: Go not into the way of the Gentiles

f.g: A people of mixed Israelite descent living between Judea and Galilee, long at odds with the Jews.

n: Israel is pictured as a flock of lost sheep needing shepherds — tying back to Jesus’s compassion in 9:36.

f.w: lost sheep of the house of Israel

n: Their message is the same one John the Baptist and Jesus preached: God’s kingdom has come near.

f.w: The kingdom of heaven is at hand

n: The apostles are to do what Jesus has done — heal, cleanse, raise, and cast out — and never charge for it. Gifts freely received should be freely shared.

f.w: freely ye have received, freely give

n: They are to take no money. Traveling without funds would teach them to rely on God and on the people they served.

f.g: Literally belts or girdles, where coins were often carried.
brass = copper coins, the lowest value.

n: No travel bag, spare clothing, or extra gear. Those who labor in God’s work deserve to be supported by those they serve.

f.g: scrip = a traveler’s bag for food.

f.w: the workman is worthy of his meat

n: In each town they should find a worthy host and stay with that family rather than moving from house to house.

f.w: there abide till ye go thence
f.g: Stay there until you leave that place.

n: On entering a home they should greet it — usually with the Hebrew blessing “Peace be to this house.”

f.g: salute = greet.

n: If the household welcomes them, their blessing of peace rests there; if not, the blessing comes back to them — nothing is lost.

f.w: let your peace return to you

n: Shaking dust off the feet was a symbolic act showing that the messengers had done their duty and the responsibility now rested on those who refused.

f.w: shake off the dust of your feet

n: Rejecting Christ’s authorized servants is serious. Sodom and Gomorrah never had such an opportunity, so their judgment will be lighter.

f.g: more bearable.

n: Jesus is honest about danger. His messengers need to be shrewd like serpents yet innocent like doves — wise without becoming harmful.

f.w: wise as serpents, and harmless as doves

f.g: Greek akeraios — pure, unmixed, without guile.

n: Persecution is coming. Local Jewish councils will try them, and they will be whipped in synagogues.

f.g: Local Jewish courts (sanhedrins).
scourge = whip.

n: They will even stand before Gentile rulers — and these trials will become opportunities to bear witness of Christ.
When on trial they shouldn’t panic about what to say; the words they need will be given in the moment.

f.g: take no thought = don’t be anxious.

n: The Holy Spirit himself will speak through them. This is a promise of divine help, not an excuse to skip preparation.
The gospel will divide even families, with some members turning others over to persecutors.

f.w: the brother shall deliver up the brother

n: Disciples will be hated because they bear Christ’s name, but those who stay faithful to the end will be saved.

f.w: he that endureth to the end shall be saved

n: When persecuted, they may move on. Jesus adds a much-discussed saying: they won’t finish reaching Israel’s towns before the Son of Man comes.

f.w: till the Son of man be come
f.g: Interpreted variously — as Jesus coming to join them, his resurrection, Jerusalem’s fall, or his Second Coming.

n: Students don’t outrank their teacher. If Jesus was persecuted, his followers should expect the same.

f.w: The disciple is not above his master

n: If enemies called the Master “Beelzebub,” his servants shouldn’t be surprised at being slandered too.

f.g: A name for Satan; probably from Baal-zebub, a Philistine god, mocked as “lord of the flies.”
The head of the household — here Jesus himself.

n: Don’t be afraid of opponents. Truth will come out; everything hidden will eventually be revealed.

f.w: nothing covered, that shall not be revealed

n: What Jesus teaches them privately they must proclaim openly. Flat rooftops were places to make public announcements.
Persecutors can only kill the body. The One to revere is God, who has power over the eternal soul.

f.g: Here fear means deep reverence and awe for God, the final Judge.
Greek Gehenna — the valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem, a symbol of judgment.

n: Sparrows were among the cheapest things sold in the market, yet God notices even when one falls.

f.g: A small copper coin (Greek assarion), worth about 1/16 of a day’s wage.
Without your Father knowing or caring.

n: God knows us in astonishing detail — down to the number of hairs on our heads.

f.w: the very hairs of your head are all numbered

n: If God cares for sparrows, he surely cares for his children. That knowledge drives out fear.

f.w: ye are of more value than many sparrows

n: Those who openly stand up for Christ will find him standing up for them before the Father.

f.g: confess = openly acknowledge, declare loyalty.

n: The reverse is also true: to deny him before others is to cut ourselves off from his advocacy.
Jesus brings inner peace, but his message also divides — people will take sides for and against him.

f.g: A symbol of division, not literal violence. Luke has “division.”

n: Jesus quotes Micah to show how faith in him can split families when some accept and others oppose.

f.g: at variance = in conflict, divided.

n: Sometimes the hardest opposition comes from those closest to us.

f.w: a man's foes shall be they of his own household

n: Love for Christ must come before every other love, even family. Rightly ordered, that love strengthens our families rather than weakening them.

f.w: loveth father or mother more than me

n: Before his own crucifixion, Jesus says disciples must take up their cross — willing to bear sacrifice and even shame to follow him.

f.g: The JST of Matthew 16:26 explains taking up the cross as denying oneself all ungodliness and keeping the commandments.

n: A central paradox of discipleship: clinging to our own life loses it, but giving our life to Christ gains true, eternal life.

f.w: loseth his life for my sake shall find it

n: To welcome Christ’s messengers is to welcome Christ himself, and through him the Father who sent him.

f.w: He that receiveth you receiveth me

n: Those who support a prophet or righteous person because of who they are share in that person’s reward.

f.w: in the name of a prophet
f.g: Because he is a prophet.

n: Even the smallest kindness — a cup of cold water — given to a humble disciple will be remembered and rewarded by God.

f.g: Humble, ordinary disciples, not only children.
